draft.title: Evaluating sources as evidence
card: A historical source is anything made or left behind that gives information about the past, such as a letter, photograph, poster or diary. A source is not evidence until a historian has asked questions about it.
Ask who made it, why, when and for whom. A source made by someone who saw the event, soon after it happened, may know more. A source made to persuade an audience may leave things out.
Check it against other sources. If several independent sources agree, the claim is more reliable. If they disagree, the historian must work out why.
A biased or one-sided source can still be useful evidence. A propaganda poster is a poor record of the facts, but it shows what its makers wanted people to believe.
draft.remember: Question a source before you trust it: who, why, when, for whom, and do others agree?

a.q: Why do historians ask why a source was made before using it as evidence?
opts: The purpose may shape what it includes or leaves out
A source made for a purpose is always false
Only sources made for private use count as evidence
The purpose shows the exact date it was made
a.why: A source made to persuade or to defend someone may stress some things and skip others, so a historian must allow for this. It does not make the source false: it can still be useful evidence once its purpose is understood.
a.clue: Think about what a maker trying to persuade might choose to leave out.

b.q: In 1916, a government in Australia issued a poster urging men to enlist. A student wants to use it as evidence. Which use is best supported by the poster alone?
opts: It shows what the government wanted people to believe
It proves how most men felt about the war
It proves how many men enlisted that year
It is useless because it was made to persuade
b.why: A poster made to persuade is good evidence of what its makers wanted people to think. It cannot prove how most men felt or how many enlisted without other sources to back it up. Its purpose does not make it useless, because a one-sided source can still be useful.
b.clue: A source made to persuade can still tell you about the persuaders.

a.best: The purpose may shape what it includes or leaves out

b.best: It shows what the government wanted people to believe
